title: Prototyping
body:
A **prototype** is built to be tested and then discarded. Its value is in how early it produces
evidence, and evidence is cheapest before anything is implemented.

**Low fidelity** is paper sketches and [[Wireframe|wireframes]]. It costs minutes, shows layout
and flow, and can be redrawn during the session in front of the user. Its disposability is the
point: a prototype somebody spent a week on gets defended in a meeting, and one drawn in five
minutes gets thrown away without argument.

**High fidelity** is an interactive mockup that behaves enough to be used, built once the
layout questions are settled. It tests things paper cannot, including timing, transitions and
whether a control is discoverable, and it costs enough that it should not be the first thing
built.

```
paper sketch      minutes     layout, flow, vocabulary
wireframe         hours       structure and hierarchy, no visual design
interactive mock  days        discoverability, timing, real interaction
built system      weeks       everything, and too late to change the structure
```

The cost of a change rises steeply along that list, which is the same argument the [[SDLC]]
makes about defects found late. A structural mistake caught on paper costs a redraw and the
same mistake caught after implementation costs the implementation.

Testing a prototype is [[Usability Testing]] with the same discipline, including the rule
that the person running the session gives the task and then stays silent.
